# The story of Blackbird: *Javelin’s* first highly automated truck


## How we gave a Peterbilt 579 an *autonomous* upgrade


[Addwiteey Chrungoo](https://medium.com/@achrungoo?source=post_page---byline--197659e1b4f0---------------------------------------)


5 min read


·


May 21, 2023


--


At[Javelin](https://www.javelinrobotics.com/) , our mission is to make freight transportation more sustainable and efficient. We’re building autonomous trucking software (and hardware) which a **human driver can easily tag-team with** .


Autonomous trucking has a lot to do with exceptional quality AI software, but also body modifications, steering columns, wire harnesses and more. The *get your hands dirty* type of engineering. Today, we wanted to share the story of how we gave our Peterbilt 579 an *autonomous* upgrade — and shed some light on what happens behind the scenes in an autonomous truck startup.

The day we signed the lease on Blackbird. It’s some 20F outside. Missing Pat here. From left: Addy, Sri, Mike, Sandesh


**How our truck sees the world**


At Javelin, we use a combination of RGB cameras, thermal cameras, radar, LIDARs and more as our choice of sensors. These sensors give our truck redundant coverage and situational awareness needed to drive autonomously.


**The design phase: Measure twice, cut once**


Before making any modifications to our vehicle, we wanted to plan, take measurements and visualize everything in software — so we started building 3D CAD models. It also helped to get things measured just about right, before sending out parts for manufacturing. We wanted most of our sensors to be somewhere near the top visor of the truck. So, we had to choose whether:


- We keep the truck’s visor and work around it
- Replace the visor with something custom


We ultimately chose to keep it simple and replace the visor with an in-house custom design. We jokingly started calling it the crown. It gave us much needed flexibility and we could use the existing mounting infrastructure on the truck. Super clean.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Top view of the crown


Next we designed mounts for the[Ouster LIDARs](https://ouster.com/) , as well as casings for the long and medium range LIDAR pairs. The Ousters were to be placed on each side of the truck, while the long & medium range LIDAR pair were to be mounted in the centre. Trucks typically generate significant vibrations, so we also incorporated some dampening around the mounts to reduce impact.

**The prototype phase: Getting parts manufactured**


Once we were confident our designs would work for the development we had planned, we got the parts professionally manufactured and shipped to us by our friends at[OSHCut](https://www.oshcut.com/) in Utah. They came well recommended and shipped us parts in no time. We also did some DIY work and final touches, which was loads of fun.

**The assembly phase: Putting it all up together**


While designing in software was fun, seeing it all become real was a tad bit more exciting. But the assembly phase was also the hardest, as we now needed to work with atoms and not bits — and modify our vehicle, for real. Mistakes could be costly!


First up to mount was the front facing radar. This was relatively easy. We drilled it to the vehicle body, and it worked out great.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Front radar


**Up next to fit was the crown.**


Attaching the crown wasn’t straightforward, especially because it was heavy and it needed to be mounted at an exact level plane. We knew we had to get this right, as most of the sensor stack was to be placed on it. The setup had to be stable, weather proof and also ruggedized enough to handle real world truck driving.


Once the crown was attached, next up was adding all the sensors, drilling the fibreglass roof to make way for wiring and ensure everything is leakproof.

All the work here was done in-house in our garage in Toronto. It was consistently 20F outside


**The wiring phase: Opening up the insides**


We pretty much opened up the entire truck from the inside, including the roof, dashboards, steering column, flooring etc. We routed wires, connected our array of ruggedized computers, power distribution systems, emergency stop and a host of other requirements.


Press enter or click to view image in full size


Press enter or click to view image in full size


We drilled into the fibreglass roof and got all sensor wires from the crown into the truck. Let’s just say seeing a C$250K truck opened up is humbling.


**The final phase: Give the truck a much-needed drive-by-wire conversion and final touches**


Unlike several cars that come with electronically controllable steering, brakes and gas — trucks don’t always have all three. To control the vehicle, we gave it a drive-by-wire conversion.
